Armed Conflict & Security
• Russia launched its largest strikes on Ukraine’s power infrastructure since spring, killing several and damaging the grid around Kyiv as winter looms.
• The U.S. and U.K. completed their troop withdrawals from Iraq, formally ending the anti-IS mission after years of drawdowns.
• A Flydubai jet bound for Israel diverted to Saudi Arabia after an onboard cockpit incident, prompting brief hijacking fears and heightened regional aviation tensions.
• Somali piracy resurfaced with deadly consequences, as an official said pirates killed an oil tanker crew before a naval rescue.
• North and South Korea exchanged threats after a landmine blast in the DMZ injured South Korean soldiers, underscoring persisting peninsula tensions.
Why it matters: Escalating attacks on Ukraine’s grid, shifting security postures in Iraq, and renewed maritime and aviation incidents highlight brittle regional stability and global spillover risks.

Economy & Markets
• OpenAI is reportedly seeking $30 billion in fresh funding at a $1.4 trillion valuation ahead of a potential 2027 listing, signaling investors’ appetite for AI despite regulatory and public sentiment swings.
• Russia extended its diesel export ban amid refinery disruptions and war-related risks, while the White House weighs U.S. export limits to manage domestic fuel prices before midterms.
• U.S. mortgage rates climbed to 7.3%, a near three-year high, as investors awaited PCE inflation data and Micron’s results; futures were steady.
• Dangote launched a Kenya oil refinery project despite land protests, positioning it as part of Africa industrialization plans.
• Manchester City’s guilty verdict on Premier League financial breaches spurred questions about penalties and potential relegation scenarios.
Why it matters: Energy policy moves, high borrowing costs, and outsized AI financings are reshaping markets and corporate strategies as consumers and investors navigate tighter financial conditions.

Climate & Environment
• California is preparing for a “Kelvin wave” and associated sea-level rise that could inundate parts of the coast by early October, amplifying climate risks through winter.
• A European Union monitor found one-third of the global population was exposed to extremely high ozone pollution this year due to heat waves, wildfires and emissions.
• Scientists are testing unconventional interventions—like soundscapes and probiotics—to help coral reefs survive a super El Niño’s heat stress.
• New South Wales approved its largest-ever coal project despite climate concerns, citing economic benefits through 2045, drawing backlash from environmental groups.
• Australia’s EV demand surged, with one electric vehicle sold roughly every 100 seconds in the first half of 2026.
Why it matters: Extreme climate signals are converging with policy trade-offs, forcing communities and governments to balance immediate economic interests against mounting environmental and public health costs.

Society & Human Rights
• Indonesia demolished a controversial “luxury prison” compound after public outcry over preferential treatment behind bars.
• Singapore launched a state-run matchmaking service for public servants amid record-low fertility, part of broader social policy efforts.
• South Africa’s president ordered a crackdown on unsafe streets after the murders of 12 women near Johannesburg sparked outrage over gender-based violence.
• A high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Spain prompted mass protests and government measures targeting the housing crisis.
• Rights groups condemned an Iranian court’s upholding of 74 lashes for a singer who performed without a hijab, calling it a form of torture.
Why it matters: Governments face intensifying pressure to address inequities, public safety, demographic challenges, and civil liberties as individual cases catalyze systemic debates.

Entertainment
• Actor Chad Lowe and his family announced the death of his 13-year-old daughter Fiona, prompting an outpouring of condolences.
• Microsoft introduced Xbox Mythic Achievements, akin to PlayStation’s Platinum trophies, rewarding players who complete all base achievements in a game.
• The Gaza war documentary “NAZA” debuted at No. 1 at the Italian box office, outpacing a re-release of “Avengers: Endgame Encore.”
• Danny Boyle said a third “28 Years Later” film has a strong script and “a lot of Cillian Murphy” and backed Jack O’Connell as a future James Bond.
• Fashion houses unveiled Spring 2027 ready-to-wear collections, with industry attention on creative leadership changes and runway debuts.
Why it matters: The industry is balancing somber news and evolving fan engagement with fresh franchises, global box office surprises, and shifting fashion calendars.

Sports
• The Republic of Ireland will play their second Nations League match against Israel as scheduled, despite public opposition and security concerns.
• Oman reached the Gulf Cup semi-finals via a drawing of lots after a dead tie with Iraq, an unusual progression method.
• Esteban Ocon will leave Haas, casting uncertainty over the French driver’s Formula 1 future heading into next season.
• Ireland will host England at Dublin’s Aviva Stadium in the 2027 Women’s Six Nations, signaling growing demand for marquee women’s rugby venues.
Why it matters: Scheduling and fairness quirks, venue upgrades, and contract moves highlight how sport navigates political sensitivities, fan expectations, and athlete careers.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Benjamin Netanyahu’s campaign faces renewed scrutiny over alleged warnings before Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, with elections weeks away.
• A planned Trump–Xi archive visit was reportedly altered due to Chinese objections around a Taiwan-related document, underscoring ongoing sensitivities.
• The UK–France “one in, one out” migrant returns deal is set to lapse amid French calls for an EU-wide approach, complicating Channel migration policy.
• UK PM Andy Burnham floated the possibility of rejoining the EU as the government reviews ties with the bloc, hinting at a longer-term rethink.
Why it matters: Domestic politics and cross-border arrangements are being tested by migration, historical narratives, and alliances, shaping Europe’s and Asia’s diplomatic contours.

Artificial Intelligence
• A Tokyo court ruled that AI-cloned voices violate publicity rights, siding with actor Kenjiro Tsuda in a landmark voice-protection case.
• The Bank of England governor said authorities must retain the “right to intervene” in AI as rogue model risks to finance rise.
• OpenAI unveiled “Dots,” always-on AI agents to automate tasks across apps, while continuing to manage fallout from recent agent-related hacks and legal challenges.
• Sam Altman said an OpenAI IPO will wait until better safety assurances are possible; separately, Trump issued an order to label AI “Super Intelligence.”
• Reports indicate OpenAI faces a lawsuit over the Hugging Face hack, testing liability for actions by autonomous systems.
Why it matters: Legal, regulatory, and product shifts are converging as policymakers weigh intervention, courts codify rights, and labs push agentic AI into everyday workflows.

Science & Technology
• Cloudflare will issue quantum-safe TLS certificates, part of a broader overhaul to future-proof web authentication against quantum attacks.
• Studies show connected cars and their apps expose users to extensive tracking, raising fresh concerns over data privacy in vehicles.
• Leaks suggest Google’s Pixel 11A will largely retain the prior midrange design, while NASA added Blue Origin’s New Glenn to its launch services catalog.
• A robot dog completed a marathon on a single charge, pointing to progress in energy efficiency and robotics endurance.
Why it matters: Security standards, consumer privacy, incremental device updates, and robotics breakthroughs underscore the pace and breadth of tech’s real-world impacts.

Health & Pandemic
• A triple-hormone obesity drug, retatrutide, yielded up to 25% weight loss in trials, bolstering the next wave of anti-obesity therapies.
• GMA anchor Will Reeve disclosed a testicular cancer diagnosis, crediting early detection and raising awareness of men’s health vigilance.
Why it matters: Advances in metabolic medicine and public figures sharing health journeys can accelerate prevention, treatment uptake, and health literacy.
https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/09/most-powerful-obesity-drug-yet-people-lost-up-to-25-of-weight-in-trial/
https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lifestyle/lifestyle-news/gma-anchor-will-reeve-testicular-cancer-diagnosis-1236716787/

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Researchers are advancing protocols for mitochondrial transplantation, aiming to improve function in aged tissues as the field moves from early studies toward broader availability.
• Experts caution that mTOR inhibition’s benefits depend heavily on context, even as rapamycin gains popularity among longevity enthusiasts.
• Transplanted hearts appear to shift toward recipients’ molecular age, suggesting host factors may influence graft epigenetics and function.
• A prevention strategy for Alzheimer’s is in clinical trials, reflecting momentum toward earlier intervention in neurodegenerative disease.
• Fruit fly studies indicate larval protein intake influences adult longevity, highlighting developmental diet’s lasting effects.
Why it matters: As interventions move from lab to clinic, understanding mechanisms, context, and biomarkers will be vital to safely extend healthspan and tailor therapies.

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/09/fruit-flies-remember-their-larval-diet-which-influences-their-longevity/

Other
• New research links snakes’ appearances to human reactions—fear, disgust, or admiration—suggesting visual traits shape perceived threat and appeal.
• Family members of Michele and Rob Reiner reflected on their deaths amid an ongoing criminal case against their son, underscoring public grief around a high-profile tragedy.
Why it matters: Understanding perception informs education and conservation, while high-profile cases test public compassion and the justice process.
https://phys.org/news/2026-09-snakes-linked-scary-appealing-people.html

Art & Culture
• Creators behind series tackling far-right politics, climate crises, and social issues discussed drama’s power—and limits—to catalyze change at Iberseries.
• Producers of “Heated Rivalry” launched the Irina Foundation to promote inclusivity and mental well-being through sport and arts programs.
• Yes keyboardist Rick Wakeman played a private concert for 150 rescue bears in Vietnam, spotlighting animal welfare and the fight against bile farming.
• Artist Wangari Mathenge’s new show at Lévy Gorvy Dayan explores identity through painting and debut sculptures co-created with her mother’s circle in Nairobi.
• InScope, a reimagined Miami art fair, debuts during Art Week with programming designed to deepen artist–collector connections.
Why it matters: Culture can galvanize audiences and philanthropy, bridging activism, identity, and market dynamics to shape public discourse.

Entertainment.title: Maison Margiela’s Tokyo-Exclusive REPLICA Fragrance Smells Like an Unsent Letter
Entertainment.text: SummaryMaison Margiela’s “Letter Never Sent” captures the intimacy of an unsent message through a Tokyo 1995-inspired scent.Sumi ink, red cedarwood and white musk evoke ink, paper and lingering emotion.The Tokyo-exclusive fragrance launches October 1.Maison Margiela turns an unfinished thought into an olfactory memory with REPLICA “Letter Never Sent,” the house’s first fragrance created exclusively for Tokyo and the first Eau de Parfum within its REPLICA Memory Collection.Set in “Tokyo, 1995,” the woody-musky composition looks back to a moment when communication was beginning to shift from the physical to the digital: handwritten letters and faxed pages giving way to emails, while words once committed to paper could increasingly disappear as easily as a deleted draft. Against the glow and restless movement of the city, “Letter Never Sent” imagines something quieter — an unposted letter kept close, preserving feelings that were written down but never delivered.That scent unfolds through a deliberately restrained trio of notes. A sumi ink accord opens with a dry, mineral transparency and faint metallic sharpness, recalling the moment fresh ink meets white paper while mirroring the cool polish of Tokyo’s urban landscape. As that initial edge settles, red cedarwood introduces warmth, grain and depth, shifting the scene from neon-lit streets toward the intimacy of a desk late at night. White musk finally softens the composition into something clean and close to the skin, evoking the smooth sensation of fine paper between the fingers. The fragrance treats the unsent letter as something suspended between past and present — its ink still legible, its emotions unfinished, and its memory lingering quietly long after the city outside has moved on.The bottle retains REPLICA’s recognizable, utilitarian presentation, with its archival-style label identifying the memory as “Tokyo, 1995,” almost like a date and place recorded on a piece of correspondence. The understated treatment allows the ink-and-paper narrative to remain central, while the wider launch extends that tactile language through a GINZA SIX concept store inspired by old postal spaces, alongside details including a takuhon-inspired furoshiki and sumi-paper pouch offered as part of the launch experience.The Maison Margiela REPLICA “Letter Never Sent” arrives October 1, 2026 in a 100ml format for ¥31,900 JPY (approx. $203 USD). The fragrance will be available exclusively through select Maison Margiela Fragrances locations and fashion boutiques in Tokyo, with no regular sales through the brand’s Japanese online store.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Erling Haaland's New Nike Phantom 6 Low Elite Only Shows Its True Colors When It Gets Wet
Entertainment.text: Name: Nike Phantom 6 Low Elite "Erling Haaland"Colorway: Baltic Blue/Glacier Blue/Blue EclipseSKU: HQ2332-401MSRP: $280 USDRelease Date: October 1Where to Buy: NikeNike is giving Erling Haaland a cleat that changes with the weather. The Phantom 6 Low Elite "Erling Haaland" arrives in Baltic Blue/Glacier Blue/Blue Eclipse. It pairs a water-activated color-changing upper with the performance package of Nike's precision-focused silhouette, and the whole concept is built around water as a metaphor for how the striker plays.The headline feature only appears once the grass is wet. The upper is printed with white ink that disappears on contact with water, revealing the full graphic hidden underneath. Nike ties the effect to Haaland himself, casting the reveal as a picture of a player who turns into something defenders can't contain. Dry, the cleat reads as a clean study in icy blues. Wet, it shows everything.That dual nature follows Nike's broader framing of Haaland as water: constantly shifting, capable of stillness one moment and a surge the next. The cold-toned palette of Baltic, Glacier, and Eclipse blues keeps the theme consistent before a single drop hits the upper.Underneath the concept, the construction is built for touch. Nike's Gripknit forms the upper, a tacky textured material designed to hold the ball whether conditions are wet or dry. It's a fitting pairing for a cleat that literally responds to rain, since the surface that changes appearance also keeps its grip when the weather turns.Traction and fit round out the spec sheet. A Cyclone 360 circular stud pattern sits in the forefoot to help players plant and pivot quickly. The shoe's frame is shaped for a more anatomical fit, particularly through the toe box, molding to the foot and bringing the wearer closer to the ball on strikes. Nike positions the Phantom 6 as an upgrade over the Phantom GX 2, with refined Gripknit touch zones, the more natural toe-box fit, and an improved Cyclone 360 plate. A cushioned sockliner finishes the interior, and this firm-ground version is intended for dry, natural-grass fields.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Nike presents the shoe as a modern version of the running shoe Bill Bowerman built before the company even carried the Nike name, famously using his wife's waffle iron. This edition reproduces that original design in a Coconut Milk/Mosswood Brown/Fennel/Light Khaki colorway.The outsole is where the story starts. A rubber Waffle outsole anchors the shoe, and its gridded tread is the direct descendant of the pattern Bowerman first pressed out in the kitchen. The rubber gives durable traction, while the waffle pattern itself doubles as the shoe's clearest link to Nike's origins.The upper keeps things period-correct. It's built mainly from nylon, the lightweight material that defined running shoes of the era, and finished with a leather Swoosh along the side. The mix of textile and leather gives the upper a layered, textured look that separates it from the smooth, engineered surfaces of modern runners.The details stay simple inside, too. Science & Technology.title: Tech to Replace Animal Testing Is Almost Ready. Scientists Are Not
Science & Technology.text: Seventeen years ago, cell biologist Donald Ingber and his colleagues at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering submitted a paper to the journal Science describing their model human lung. It was smaller than a USB stick and made of a clear polymer slab containing narrow channels, which were lined with the type of cells that line a lung’s air sacs and blood vessels. When air was pumped through hollow chambers beside the channels, the device rhythmically expanded and contracted—it “breathed.”This lifelike movement was a dramatic change from previous generations of lung models, which typically used static cultures of lung tissue that were unable to simulate the movements essential to lung function. When exposed to inflammatory proteins and bacteria, Ingber’s artificial lung reacted much as living lungs would. And exposure to silica nanoparticles used to model the effects of ultrafine particulates revealed that movement affected how tissues absorbed them. Donald Ingber led the team that developed the first human lung-on-a-chip at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute. Sam OgdenIt was a powerful proof-of-principle demonstration of a system that could be used to test drugs and other chemicals, providing a complement and even an alternative to testing in tissue cultures or in animals. Even so, the editors at Science were hesitant. They rejected the paper and suggested that Ingber’s team also run the tests in mice.It wasn’t an unreasonable request: Harvard’s lung system was new and comparing the results it generated to results from mice would help validate it. Ingber’s team ran the suggested experiments and resubmitted their study a year later, in 2010, at which point it was published. (It has since been cited by nearly 5,400 other papers.) Still, the incident spoke to how animal models have been the default of modern biomedical research. An early lung-on-a-chip developed at Harvard’s Wyss Institute used microfluidic channels lined with human cells to reproduce key features of lung function. Wyss Institute at Harvard UniversityA recent story told by Ilka Maschmeyer, a translational toxicology researcher and executive at the German biotech company TissUse, shows how much things have changed. TissUse specializes in building organ-on-a-chip systems—the conversational name for systems like Ingber’s lung—that are used by pharmaceutical companies for research. A few months ago, says Maschmeyer, a pharmaceutical company approached TissUse after being denied permission by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to run a clinical trial of a new drug. The problem: It had presented animal data, but the FDA wanted data from organs-on-a-chip or some comparable alternative. The standards had come full circle.A Breathing Lung-on-a-ChipThe moment spoke to a trend, perhaps even the early days of a fundamental shift, away from the use of animals in toxicology and drug development. “It’s rare still,” says Maschmeyer, “but I think it’s going to be more and more frequent.”A host of these kinds of alternatives to experiments on animals have been developed over the years. Collectively they’re known as NAMs, an acronym that stands, depending on whom you’re talking to, for new approach methodologies, novel alternative methods, or nonanimal methods. Most NAMs have yet to be rigorously tested, but early studies suggest their potential.As NAMs have become more sophisticated, the question of how they will be implemented has become less about their technical qualities and more about the practical next steps needed to realize their potential. Validating NAMs—standardizing the systems, conducting head-to-head comparisons with animal experiments—is an enormous challenge. Moreover, simply outperforming animal models is necessary but not sufficient. The adoption of NAMs will require changes in policy, training, and culture.“This transition process is much more complicated than you would think,” says Thomas Hartung, a toxicologist and director of the Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing at Johns Hopkins University. “It is more about change management than it is about the technology.”The Technologies Replacing Animal TestingFor decades, animal advocates and many scientists have criticized both the morality and usefulness of experimenting on animals. An estimated 92 percent of all drugs that enter U.S. clinical trials fail to reach the market, sometimes for business reasons but often because the drugs prove ineffective or unsafe in ways that were not predicted by animal experiments. Failure rates are even higher in drugs for heart disease, cancer, and diseases of the brain.These statistics don’t automatically mean that a reliance on animals is to blame. Flawed study designs are a problem too, and also the sheer confounding complexity of disease. But there’s little question that animals have made poor surrogates for many conditions. And just as animal experiments may mistakenly suggest efficacy or fail to predict harm in humans, they might also erroneously suggest that drugs are ineffective or harmful when they could actually work in humans. Some researchers argue that if aspirin or acetaminophen had been discovered after the advent of modern testing requirements, they might have been abandoned.   TissUse’s Humimic systems use microfluidic chips to culture human tissues and model interactions between organs. A researcher images tissues in a chip during an experiment [top], Humimic chips sit in a temperature-controlled unit [center], and a researcher prepares chips for use [bottom].TissUse (3)Researchers developing NAMs have pushed these systems far beyond old-fashioned tissue cultures. The new technologies include organoids that more closely mimic the structure, composition, and function of human organs. More humanlike still are organ-on-a-chip systems; alongside Ingber’s lung-on-a-chip are brains, hearts, kidneys, and even placentas on a chip. As many as 10 such organs have been linked together, yielding multi-organ systems that promise to recapitulate many aspects of human physiology—not perfectly, but better than a mouse or a monkey would. Supporting these systems are computational simulations of organs and organisms, and also artificial intelligence tools that analyze data generated by other systems and inform future experiments in a high-powered iterative loop.Yet even as studies piled up and some pharmaceutical companies started using NAMs in-house, the U.S. regulatory system governing drug developing and testing remained an obstacle to their wider use. NAM proponents were overjoyed, then, when in late 2022 the FDA Modernization Act 2.0 passed into law. It explicitly authorized the use of NAMs in the preclinical studies required of new drugs before they could enter human trials. Previous regulations had mandated animal testing; now the door was open to alternatives. It was a landmark moment. “That was something I didn’t expect to see in my life,” says Maschmeyer.Although immediate in-the-lab impact was limited, the FDA’s decision was a harbinger of things to come. In 2025, the FDA pledged “to make animal studies the exception rather than the norm” for drug safety testing. Then, in September 2026, the agency followed up by issuing a rule that, if it takes effect, will replace references to “animal tests” in its drug-development regulations with the broader term “nonclinical tests.” The change makes explicit that validated alternatives such as human-cell systems, organs-on-chips, and computer models can be used when appropriate.Also in 2025, the U.S. National Institutes of Health, the world’s largest public biomedical research funder, announced that researchers applying for grants to study animal models would also need to incorporate nonanimal research, such as real-world data or studies of NAMs. Meanwhile, the European Commission and United Kingdom have announced their own plans to phase out animal testing, and the intergovernmental Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development updated its influential guidelines to allow for expanded use of NAMs.NAM proponents say these shifts were essential: If regulators won’t accept NAM results, there’s less incentive to adopt them, especially for researchers already working with animals. Maschmeyer says TissUse’s clients increasingly include scientists whose research has been focused on animals. “I see, within the last year, a change,” says Maschmeyer. “It’s more people who are working with animal models who now have to also add in vitro models.” She traces it mainly to the regulatory shift—a trend Ingber calls “game-changing.”Proving That NAMs WorkIt’s not enough for regulators to say that NAMs can or should be used, though. Even more important is the regulatory apparatus dedicated to assessing how they should be used. This begins with their validation: the process by which experimental methodologies and devices are determined to be reliable and trustworthy. A prototype brain-on-a-chip designed to model a rare neurological disease might work fine in the lab that developed it—but to be validated, the system needs to work in the real world.“You read about all the organ chips that come out of academic labs, which is great—but that’s not going to change their uptake by the FDA, because you have to get the same results anywhere in the world. It has to be a commercial product. It has to be mass-produced and meet very fine performance criteria,” says Ingber. For example, even minute variations in the hydrogels used as tissue scaffolds in organ chips can produce very different growth patterns. Emulate’s Organ-Chips are connected to the company’s automated culture system, which supplies the chips with nutrients and controls the flow of fluid through them. EmulateWorkflows and procedures need to be uniform, too. One obstacle to wider use of vascularized tumor-on-a-chip platforms in developing cancer therapies, for example, is the different metrics used by different research groups to characterize blood-vessel function and geometry. Experimental guidelines, workflows, checkpoints, metrics, reporting criteria: All need to be standardized in order for researchers to compare their work and collaborate across platforms. Members of Ingber’s lab coach industry researchers on how to use chips developed by Emulate, a company founded by Ingber. But even with instructions, they still need help with the finer points of tending to stem-cell cultures.When a NAM is ready for commercial use and researchers know how to use it, the most important test—whether it provides clinical benefit—still remains. A rare-disease organ chip might be reliable, but are the biomarkers it measures actually relevant? If so, are the algorithms that extrapolate chip results to the drug’s in-body effects truly predictive?    Microscopic images reveal the human tissues grown inside Emulate’s Organ-Chips. Bacteria, shown in magenta, interact with mucus and airway cells in a LungChip [top]; an IntestineChip develops structures resembling those that absorb nutrients in the small intestine [center]; and tiny hairlike cilia grow on cells in another LungChip, where they help move mucus and trapped particles out of the airway [bottom].Emulate (3)Such questions have been answered for some NAMs. For example, a liver-on-a-chip system from Emulate correctly flagged about seven out of every eight drugs that had safely passed animal trials but proved toxic to human livers. A similar study was conducted by researchers from Oxford University and Janssen Pharmaceutica (later renamed Johnson & Johnson Innovative Medicine). That team showed that their computational simulations of human heart cells flagged compounds that caused a type of dangerous heart arrhythmia with 89 percent accuracy, compared to animal studies that were 75 percent accurate.Such studies, however, are complicated and costly. Emulate’s study required 870 chips and the labor equivalent of 16 full-time employees working for 16 weeks—efforts far beyond the reach of the average lab. If the researchers wanted regulatory approval to use their chip to predict large-molecule drugs rather than the small-molecule drugs they tested, they would have needed to run another such study for that particular use. And comparable studies ostensibly need to be conducted for every commercially available NAM and every context in which they would be used—a vast undertaking. “That’s a challenge,” says Kathy Archibald, founder of Safer Medicines Trust, a United Kingdom–based group that considers animals to be poor models of human biology. “It takes too long and costs too much, and small companies can’t afford to do it.”Ingber thinks that academic scientists need to collaborate more with industry researchers on NAMs, and that governments should fund those projects. He and other NAM proponents also stress the importance of having access to the necessary data: Without information from preclinical animal studies and human clinical trials, comparisons are difficult, but much of that data is now proprietary. Pharmaceutical companies and regulators need to share it, they say, and the FDA has called for an open-access repository of drug toxicity data. Hartung of Johns Hopkins also suggests that new animal experiments be run in parallel with NAMs, producing side-by-side comparisons.To Christian Maass, a computational biologist at the German biotechnology company ESQlabs, NAMS are overdue for a showdown with animal models. His company makes “digital twin” systems in which data from organ chip systems inform whole-human simulations of drug outcomes and disease progression. “I love what we are doing,” says Maass, speaking not only of his company but of the whole field. But he adds that researchers have not yet provided “the evidence and the proof that we are doing better or as good as the animal models.”Maass thinks that head-to-head comparisons are essential to good science. After all, if a NAM doesn’t outperform an animal model, or works best as a complement rather than a replacement, that needs to be known. He also believes such studies could convince skeptics. Maass mentions the debut of the iPhone, when people saw for the first time how well a phone could work without buttons. “That was an ‘aha!’ moment,” he says. But for NAMs, “that moment is still lacking.”Changing Scientific HabitsEven when those head-to-head comparisons are made, though, and regulations are appropriately changed, adoption can be slow. In the mid-1990s, researchers developed and validated the monocyte activation test—an assay that uses human blood cells to predict immune response—to replace the rabbit pyrogen test, which involves injecting a compound into a rabbit’s ear and monitoring the animal’s rectal temperature. But it wasn’t until 2010 that the European Pharmacopeia—the official Europe-wide standards for such testing—accepted the monocyte activation test as a replacement. And rabbits are still widely used for this test worldwide.Why the slow pace of change? In part because updates to guidance documents referring to animal tests lagged behind, but also because of inertia within the culture and institutions of science. “The formal requirement may disappear, but the informal expectation persists,” says Kathrin Herrmann, a veterinary scientist and colleague of Hartung’s at the Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing. Regulators, grant reviewers, peer reviewers, journal editors—the human infrastructure of science—often still expect to see animal data and are unfamiliar with NAMs.Herrmann is now overseeing a survey of early-career researchers working with, or trying to make the switch to, NAMs. “We consistently hear concerns that NAM-only proposals are perceived as risky by funders, that there is pressure to ‘add an animal experiment’ for credibility, that access to NAM infrastructure is limited, and that career trajectories become uncertain when departing from established animal models,” says Herrmann.  The vast majority of drugs entering clinical trials in the United States fail to reach FDA approval [failure rates in pink], with particularly high failure rates in some therapeutic areas.Animal models are embedded in databases, training programs, and the very culture of research. Scientists who use animals may be reluctant to change; their identities as researchers are tied to animals and, more practically, they’ve spent their careers learning the techniques. A toxicologist who has used rats for decades might understandably look askance when asked to take a chance on unfamiliar chunks of polymer and stem cells—especially when human well-being, or millions of dollars, may ride on the choice. Likewise, an academic scientist whose career was built on animal models may not welcome NAMs; a switch may represent the loss of jobs for lab members whose expertise is no longer relevant. “I could see why it’s a hard thing for people to take it up,” says Ingber.Education and training is vital, say NAM proponents. The NIH and FDA now offer resources for researchers interested in NAMs, as do their counterparts in other countries embracing the technologies. Herrmann helps run webinars where researchers and regulators learn to use and evaluate NAMs; Hartung’s modules on Coursera, the online learning platform, have been taken by about 12,000 students so far. “These trainees will set up their own labs. They will go to industry. They will replace the old guard,” says Joseph Wu, director of Stanford University’s Cardiovascular Institute.Wu is also a cofounder of Greenstone Biosciences, a company that uses stem-cell-derived human tissues and AI to model disease and predict drug responses. He’s used that position to introduce researchers to NAMs, helping convince the company’s directors to freely share Greenstone’s large library of stem-cell lines with any academic researchers who want to use them. “I really believe that people should understand how this platform works,” says Wu. “At the end of the day, we’re just trying to advance science.”With enough time—and funding, incentives, training, education, collaboration, and generational turnover—the research culture of drug development and safety testing may shift. Whether NAMs will be used in other areas of science, though, is an open question. Early-stage drug development and regulatory testing account for roughly 30 percent of animals used in experiments; the rest are used in basic biological research. Replacing those animals is less straightforward, but it may be possible: Ingber describes organ-on-a-chip-based insights into inflammatory bowel disease, preterm birth, and treating viral infections that couldn’t have been made in animals. Hartung calls the adoption of NAMs in toxicology a “lighthouse function,” helping guide the way for other types of research.“Suddenly, all the dams have opened,” he says.

Starting on Monday, October 12, 2026, customers can initiate the brand’s signature 'Get ready' configuration process. Applying this recurring launch strategy to its very first foldable device allows Apple to proactively streamline the checkout experience, ensuring that prospective buyers can minimize technical issues and secure their devices during a high-demand pre-order window.This advance setup window gives buyers a crucial head start to pre-select their exact configuration options well before the official drop. Accessed directly through the Apple Store app and Apple's online store, the 'Get ready' process lets users lock in their preferred storage amount, wireless carrier, payment method and colorway, with the foldable device launching in sharp Night Sky and Star White options. Available wireless carrier options for the initial rollout include AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon. Once the setup is completed, customers will be positioned for a rapid checkout when official pre-orders for the iPhone Duo go live on Friday, October 16, at 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time (5:00 a.m. Pacific Time). The foldable phone will then be officially available for purchase on October 23, 2026.As Apple's first foldable smartphone, the hardware introduces an entirely new physical footprint for the tech giant. When closed, the device operates using a compact 5.4-inch outer display. Opening the physical architecture reveals a sprawling 7.6-inch inner display that utilizes a special nano-texture finish specifically designed to minimize glare. To ensure flawless visual continuity for the user as they transition between the two modes, both the inner and outer displays share the exact same aspect ratio.Under the hood, the entire experience is powered by Apple's new A20 Pro chip. The device's foundational hardware design relies on a highly engineered precision hinge and a dual-battery architecture to support the demanding dual-screen setup. To keep the powerful processor running smoothly within the folding chassis, Apple integrates an advanced thermal management system equipped with a custom-designed vapor chamber. Art & Culture.title: InScope Is a New Art Fair That Should Be on Your Radar
Art & Culture.text: SummaryInScope, formerly Scope Art Show, will open its inaugural edition from December 1 through December 6 during the upcoming Miami Art WeekThe fair is designed to make collecting personal, allowing for deeper connections between artists, galleries, and collectorsProgramming includes talks, performances, tours, wellness events, and large-scale feature projects from Alake Shilling, Aurora Mititelu, Blue Floor Project, Ceren Arslan, Jason Hackenwerth, Nurse, Rabi Towing, and SwoonInScope is the new fair joining Miami this December, and, designed for discovery, it’s looking to shake things up during the city’s upcoming Art Week.The inaugural edition will hit the sands on Ocean Drive at 8th Street between December 1 and 6, planting its indoor and outdoor art installations, gallery pavilions, and social spaces across 220,000 square feet. Built around curiosity and connection, the event introduces a new format designed to bring artists, galleries, and collectors together in encounters that feel personal. “Art gives those conversations a starting point,” said InScope’s CEO and Co-founder Matt Middleton. “Our ambition is for people to leave with the relationships they came for and the inspiration they didn’t expect.”While the full gallery list is coming soon, its day-to-night programming so far offers a promising mix of talks, performances, tours, and wellness events. And its Feature Projects roster is already looking stacked. The first wave of announced projects includes Alake Shilling (Tlaloc Studios), Aurora Mititelu, Blue Floor Project (Fuze and Baha Mar), Ceren Arslan, Jason Hackenwerth (CAMP Gallery), Nurse (Walshy Fire), Rabi Towing, and Swoon.And while this marks the debut edition, the minds behind it aren’t the new kids on the block. Headed by Middleton, Alexis Hubshman, Hayley River Smith, and the former SCOPE Art Show team, InScope leans on 25 years of championing artists and galleries to reconsider and create space for diverse perspectives and experiences. The art of collecting arrives with a sense of excitement and belonging, whether you're a first-time buyer or a seasoned pro.“There isn’t only one way to experience art,” Smith, InScope’s director and recent State of Art featuree, explained. “We want to give people reasons to spend time, ask questions, and find something that stays with them.”InScope will hold its inaugural edition from December 1 through 6 in Miami Beach.
